summary.text: Lesson 1 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words covering praise and criticism (extol, detract, bewail), freedom and hardship (emancipate, destitute, vagabond), and description (flamboyant, intermittent, insuperable, visage), plus maxim, impetus, obligatory, plumb and wheedle.

why.text: These are the words that show up in argument and analysis — extol, detract and bewail are how writers signal which side they are on without saying so outright. Learning them is partly vocabulary and partly learning to catch a writer’s thumb on the scale.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 1 words correctly
Distinguish words that carry a built-in judgement from neutral ones
Name the relationship inside a word-pair analogy and apply it
Recognize how loaded verbs shape a reader’s view of the same facts

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 1 word list. New this unit: ANALOGY questions in the standardized-test format (EXTOL : PRAISE :: ?), which the book itself uses. The skill being trained is naming the relationship — degree, antonym, type-to-category — before looking at the options, and every explanation names it explicitly rather than just giving the answer. Pronunciations on the cards are hand-checked, so the speaker button is reliable.

nextUp.text: Cards first — tap 🔊 on any word you are unsure how to say. Then the quiz.

cards.def:
**To express deep regret or sorrow over.** (verb)
• Football fans bewailed the replacement of real grass with AstroTurf.
• Stronger than 'regret' — bewailing is regret said out loud.

**Without resources or possessions, especially the necessities of life.** (adjective)
• Second meaning: lacking or devoid of — staring at the blank page, I was destitute of ideas.
• destitution (n): the state of having nothing.
cards.hint: Think "destroyed finances" — destitute is poverty at its most complete.

cards.def:
**To take away, especially from the value, beauty, or importance of.** (verb)
• The family's loud music detracts from the peace of the beach.
• detractor (n): someone who criticizes, taking away from a plan's standing.
cards.hint: de- (away) + tract (pull). It PULLS AWAY from something good.

cards.def:
**To set free from slavery; to liberate.** (verb)
• Lincoln's 1863 Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in the Confederacy free.
• Used loosely too: some teenagers feel emancipated the day they get a driver's licence.

**To praise highly.** (verb)
• The scout leader extolled the virtues of truth and honour.
• Not ordinary praise — extolling is praise turned all the way up.

**Excessively showy; unrestrained.** (adjective)
• My conservative aunt thought the boldly patterned necktie too flamboyant for the reception.
• flamboyance (n): the quality of being showy.
cards.hint: From the French for "flaming" — it draws the eye like a flame.

cards.def:
**A driving force; anything that causes an action.** (noun)
• Her hope of an athletic scholarship was the impetus for years of training.
• Second meaning: the increased activity that force produces.

**Incapable of being overcome or defeated.** (adjective)
• During my senior year, passing Physics seemed an insuperable obstacle to graduation.
• Note the built-in 'super' — nothing gets OVER it.

**Not continuous; happening at intervals.** (adjective)
• Showers were intermittent all day, although the forecast had promised sunshine.
• Stop, start, stop, start — that pattern is the whole word.

**A general truth or rule of conduct; a short saying.** (noun)
• Remember the maxim "Actions speak louder than words."
• A maxim is advice compressed to a sentence you can carry around.

**Required or demanded.** (adjective)
• Physical education is obligatory unless you have a medical excuse.
• Same root as obligation — it is the opposite of optional.

**To understand something by examining it closely; to solve.** (verb)
• Also: to measure the depth of water, or to reach the deepest part — a vessel built to plumb the oceans.
• As an adjective it means straight up and down: the bricklayer checks the wall is plumb.
cards.hint: A plumb line is a weight on a string dropped to find depth. Every meaning is about going straight DOWN into something.

cards.def:
**A person who wanders from place to place.** (noun)
• He spent a few years as a vagabond before settling in a city.
• Also an adjective: the vagabond life of travelling musicians.

**A face, especially one that expresses feelings.** (noun)
• The smiling visage of a young girl looked out from the portrait.
• Not any face — a visage is a face that is telling you something.

**To coax by using sly persuasion or insincere praise.** (verb)
• He tried to wheedle his father into letting him go out on a school night.
• Second meaning: to GAIN something that way — she wheedled the test questions out of a friend.

opts: The lead seemed insuperable until the other team scored three goals in four minutes
The insuperable rain fell steadily all afternoon
She gave an insuperable speech that moved the audience to tears
His insuperable manner made everyone at the party uncomfortable
questions.hint: Insuperable describes something that cannot be got past.
steps: Insuperable means incapable of being overcome or defeated.
A lead that "seemed insuperable" is one nobody could catch — and the sentence then subverts it.
Rain, speeches and manners can be heavy, moving or rude, but none of those is about being unbeatable.

ex.main: **A lead nobody can overcome.** Insuperable attaches to obstacles and advantages, not to weather or personality.
ex.tip: When a word contains a familiar chunk, use it: SUPER means over. Nothing gets over an insuperable barrier.

questions.q: A maxim is best described as:
opts: A short saying that states a general truth or rule of conduct
A driving force behind an action
A person who moves from town to town
An expression of deep sorrow
questions.hint: Think of a proverb printed on a poster.
steps: A maxim is a compact statement of a general truth.
"Actions speak louder than words" is a maxim: short, general, and offered as guidance.
The other options define impetus, vagabond and bewail.

ex.main: **A short saying carrying a general truth.** Its brevity is the point — a maxim is meant to be remembered whole.
ex.tip: Three of these options are also Lesson 1 words. Eliminating by definition beats guessing by feel.

questions.q: What does it mean to extol something?
opts: To praise it highly
To take away from its value
To require it of everyone
To examine it closely for meaning
questions.hint: It is praise, but not mild praise.
steps: Extol means to praise highly.
The scout leader extolling truth and honour is not mentioning them — he is elevating them.
The wrong options belong to detract, obligatory and plumb.

ex.main: **To praise highly.** Ordinary praise is "praise"; extol reserves itself for the version turned up loud.
ex.tip: Extol and detract sit at opposite ends of the same scale. Learning them as a pair costs half the effort.

opts: A porch light that flickers on and off through the evening
A porch light that stays on all night
A porch light that has burned out completely
A porch light that is brighter than the neighbours’
steps: Intermittent means happening at intervals rather than continuously.
A light flickering on and off is the definition rendered as a picture.
Staying on is continuous, burning out is neither, and brightness is a different quality entirely.

ex.main: **The flickering light.** Intermittent is about the PATTERN over time, not the strength of the thing.
ex.tip: If a word describes how something behaves over time, test each option by playing it forward in your head.

questions.q: A person described as destitute is:
opts: Lacking the basic necessities of life
Wandering from place to place
Excessively showy in dress
Required to attend
questions.hint: It is about having nothing, not going nowhere.
steps: Destitute means without resources or possessions, especially necessities.
The word is about what someone LACKS, not where they are or how they look.
The wrong options define vagabond, flamboyant and obligatory.

ex.main: **Lacking life’s necessities.** Destitution is the noun — the state the potato famine forced on Irish families.
ex.tip: Destitute and vagabond both suggest hardship and get confused. One is about poverty; the other about movement.

questions.q: To plumb a mystery is to:
opts: Understand it by examining it closely
Announce it publicly
Make it seem less important
Set it aside for later
questions.hint: Think about a weight dropped to find the bottom.
steps: Plumb literally means to measure the depth of water.
Figuratively it means to reach the deepest part of something — to plumb the human soul.
Applied to a mystery it means examining it closely enough to reach the bottom of it.

ex.main: **To understand it by examining it closely.** Every sense of plumb runs the same direction: straight down to the bottom.
ex.tip: A word with a literal and a figurative sense usually keeps the same shape in both. Find the shape, keep the word.

opts: Sly persuasion or insincere flattery
Direct and forceful demands
Silent disapproval
Careful measurement
questions.hint: What kind of persuasion has an agenda hidden in it?
steps: To wheedle is to coax using sly persuasion or insincere praise.
The insincerity is essential — wheedling is flattery pointed at a goal.
Forceful demands are the opposite approach; the other options are unrelated.

ex.main: **Sly persuasion or insincere flattery.** If the praise is genuine, it is not wheedling.
ex.tip: Watch for words where the SPEAKER’S MOTIVE is baked into the definition. That is usually what a test question targets.

questions.q: A city council member argues that a proposed glass tower "detracts from the historic character of the square." She means the tower would:
opts: Diminish something valuable that is already there
Physically block the road through the square
Cost more than the city can afford
Require approval from the state government
questions.hint: Detract is about value, not money or logistics.
steps: Detract means to take away from the value, beauty or importance of something.
The square already HAS historic character; the tower would reduce it.
Cost and permits might be real objections, but they are not what this word claims.

ex.main: **It would diminish something valuable already present.** Detract always needs an existing quality to subtract from.
ex.tip: Precision matters in arguments: "detracts from" is a claim about value, and answering it requires defending value.

opts: A near miss on the highway was the impetus for her defensive-driving course
The impetus of the lake made it impossible to swim across
He spoke with such impetus that no one dared interrupt
The museum’s impetus dated to the eighteenth century
steps: An impetus is a driving force — the thing that sets an action going.
A near miss causing someone to sign up for a course is exactly that: cause, then action.
The other sentences reach for depth, forcefulness and age, none of which impetus means.

ex.main: **The near miss drove her to act.** An impetus is upstream of a decision; you should be able to point at what it caused.
ex.tip: Test an impetus sentence by asking "what action resulted?" If nothing followed, the word is being misused.

questions.q: A reviewer writes that an actor’s performance was "flamboyant to the point of distraction." The reviewer is saying the performance was:
opts: So showy that it pulled attention away from the play
So quiet that the audience struggled to hear
Technically skilled but emotionally cold
Faithful to the playwright’s original intent
steps: Flamboyant means excessively showy or unrestrained.
"To the point of distraction" tells you the showiness cost something.
What it cost was the audience’s attention to the play itself.

ex.main: **Showy enough to steal focus from the play.** Flamboyant already leans critical; the phrase that follows confirms it.
ex.tip: Some words carry a verdict inside them. Flamboyant is rarely neutral — notice which way a word tilts before you use it.

questions.q: Attendance at the assembly is obligatory. This means students:
opts: Are required to attend
Are encouraged but not required to attend
May attend only with a signed permission form
Will be rewarded for attending
steps: Obligatory means required or demanded.
It removes the choice — that is the whole force of the word.
Encouragement, permission and reward all leave the decision with the student; obligatory does not.

ex.main: **They are required to attend.** Obligatory is the flat opposite of optional, with no middle ground.
ex.tip: Look for the root you already know. Obligation lives inside obligatory and gives the meaning away.

opts: bewail : regret
detract : add
visage : face
vagabond : travel
questions.hint: How is extolling different from ordinary praising? Same difference, same direction.
steps: First work out the stem’s relationship: to extol is to praise INTENSELY.
So the pattern is: first word = an extreme form of the second.
Test each pair. To bewail is to regret intensely — a match.
Detract and add are opposites; visage and face are near-synonyms; a vagabond is a person, not a stronger form of travel.

ex.main: **Both pairs are DEGREE: the first word is the intense version of the second.** Extol is praise turned up; bewail is regret turned up.
ex.tip: Always name the relationship in a sentence before looking at the options. "X is an extreme form of Y" is a sentence you can test.

opts: vagabond : wanderer
extol : criticize
flamboyant : showiness
impetus : movement
questions.hint: Is a maxim a KIND of saying, or the opposite of one?
steps: A maxim is a particular type of saying — one stating a general truth.
So the relationship is: specific type to its general category.
A vagabond is a specific type of wanderer. Match.
Extol and criticize are opposites, flamboyant names a quality rather than a category, and impetus causes movement.

ex.main: **Both pairs are TYPE TO CATEGORY: the first is a specific kind of the second.** Every maxim is a saying; every vagabond is a wanderer.
ex.tip: The type-to-category test: can you say "every A is a B, but not every B is an A"? If yes, that is the relationship.

opts: obligatory : optional
maxim : proverb
extol : praise
vagabond : road
questions.hint: These two describe opposite ends of the same quality.
steps: Flamboyant means unrestrained showiness, so the stem pair is opposites.
The relationship is: first word means the reverse of the second.
Obligatory (required) and optional (free choice) are exact opposites. Match.
Maxim and proverb are synonyms, extol intensifies praise, and a road is where a vagabond travels.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ANTONYMS.** Flamboyant and restrained sit at opposite ends of showiness; obligatory and optional at opposite ends of choice.
ex.tip: When a stem looks like opposites, check that the WRONG options are not opposites too. Here only one pair reverses.

opts: emancipate : bondage
plumb : depth
bewail : sorrow
wheedle : flattery
questions.hint: What does detracting DO to value? Look for a pair doing the same thing.
steps: To detract is to take value AWAY — the verb removes the noun.
So the pattern is: the verb eliminates the thing named.
To emancipate is to remove bondage. Match.
Plumb measures depth, bewail expresses sorrow, and wheedling uses flattery — measuring, expressing and using are not removing.

ex.main: **Both pairs are VERB REMOVES NOUN.** Detracting takes away value; emancipating takes away bondage.
ex.tip: Verb-and-noun pairs hide several different relationships — removes, measures, expresses, uses. Say which one out loud before choosing.

questions.q: A biographer writes: "His detractors bewailed the appointment; his admirers extolled it." What does this sentence establish about the appointment?
opts: It divided opinion sharply, with strong feeling on both sides
It was universally unpopular
It was met mostly with indifference
It was reversed shortly after being announced
questions.hint: Three Lesson 1 words are doing the work. Sort them by who is speaking.
steps: Detractors are critics; they bewailed — expressed deep sorrow over — the appointment.
Admirers extolled it — praised it highly.
Both verbs are intense, and they point in opposite directions.
So the appointment split opinion, and neither side was lukewarm.

ex.main: **Sharply divided opinion, strongly felt on both sides.** The intensity of BOTH verbs is what rules out indifference.
ex.tip: When a sentence pairs two loaded verbs against each other, the structure itself is the answer — read the shape, not just the words.

questions.q: Two students describe the same classmate. One says she "wheedled" an extension from the teacher; the other says she "explained her situation and received" one. What does the word choice reveal?
opts: The first speaker sees the request as manipulative; the second sees it as honest
The first speaker thinks the extension was denied
The two are describing different classmates
The first speaker believes the teacher acted unfairly
questions.hint: Wheedle carries a judgement about the asker’s sincerity.
steps: Both sentences describe the same outcome: she asked, she got the extension.
But wheedle means to coax with SLY or INSINCERE persuasion.
Choosing that verb accuses her of manipulating the teacher; "explained her situation" grants her honesty.
The facts are identical, so the difference lives entirely in the speakers’ judgement of her.

ex.main: **The first speaker judges the request manipulative; the second judges it honest.** Same event, opposite verdicts — carried by one verb.
ex.tip: Loaded verbs smuggle opinions into sentences that look factual. Spotting them is most of what close reading is.

questions.q: Which pair of Lesson 1 words could describe the SAME obstacle from opposite attitudes?
opts: insuperable and surmountable — one says it cannot be beaten, the other that it can
obligatory and required — both say the same thing
maxim and adage — both mean a short saying
visage and face — both name the same thing
questions.hint: Which of these pairs actually disagrees?
steps: The question asks for words describing one obstacle from OPPOSITE attitudes.
Insuperable claims the obstacle cannot be overcome; surmountable claims it can.
The other pairs are synonyms — they agree rather than disagree, so they cannot express opposite attitudes.

ex.main: **Insuperable and surmountable.** Calling the same obstacle insuperable or surmountable is a claim about the person facing it, not just the obstacle.
ex.tip: Whether an obstacle is "insuperable" is often an argument in disguise. Notice when a description is really a prediction.
